claims.text: The modeled material is a single-crystal equiatomic FeNiCrMn alloy with an FCC structure.
The simulation cell contains approximately 180,000 atoms and uses periodic boundary conditions.
Yielding under uniaxial tension is controlled by dislocation nucleation at vacancy clusters.
Plastic deformation is mediated by 1/6<112> Shockley partial dislocations.
Shockley partial dislocations generate intrinsic and extrinsic stacking faults.
The stacking faults produce localized HCP-like regions without a bulk phase transformation.
The alloy will be loaded along <110>, <1-12>, and <-111> crystallographic directions.
The comparison will span temperatures of 10 K, 300 K, and 600 K and strain rates of 10^8, 10^9, and 10^10 s^-1.
Yielding is marked by a sudden stress drop associated with dislocation nucleation at vacancy sites.
Increasing temperature enhances atomic vibrations and facilitates dislocation nucleation.
Temperature-assisted dislocation nucleation reduces yield strength.
Increasing strain rate raises dislocation density because kinetic limitations suppress dislocation annihilation.
Yield strength is negligibly sensitive to strain rate between 10^8 and 10^10 s^-1.
The <-111> loading orientation produces the maximum yield stress among the tested orientations.
No FCC-to-BCC transformation occurs under the specified simulations.
No deformation twinning occurs under the specified simulations.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-crystal FCC equiatomic FeNiCrMn under the stated molecular-dynamics loading conditions and strain-rate range.
DXA and CNA can distinguish dislocation-mediated stacking-fault formation from twinning or a bulk phase transformation.
